cemc-fryer-2021-01a.title: Count unit squares
cemc-fryer-2021-01a.body:
The card can be split into 5 rows of 9 one-centimetre squares: $5 \times 9 = 45$ squares, so 45 cm².

**Answer: 45 cm²**

cemc-fryer-2021-01b.title: Compare areas
cemc-fryer-2021-01b.body:
The page has area $20 \times 27 = 540$ cm². With no waste, the number of cards is $540 \div 45 = 12$.

**Answer: 12**

cemc-fryer-2021-01b.title: Arrange them
cemc-fryer-2021-01b.body:
Put the 5 cm sides along the 20 cm edge and the 9 cm sides along the 27 cm edge: $20 \div 5 = 4$ across and $27 \div 9 = 3$ down, so $4 \times 3 = 12$ cards fill the page exactly.

**Answer: 12**

cemc-fryer-2021-01c.title: Count each layout
cemc-fryer-2021-01c.body:
**Portrait:** across the 19 cm edge we fit $\lfloor 19/5 \rfloor = 3$ cards ($4 \times 5 = 20 > 19$); along the 29 cm edge $\lfloor 29/9 \rfloor = 3$ cards ($4 \times 9 = 36 > 29$). That is $3 \times 3 = 9$ cards.

**Landscape:** across the 19 cm edge $\lfloor 19/9 \rfloor = 2$ cards; along the 29 cm edge $\lfloor 29/5 \rfloor = 5$ cards. That is $2 \times 5 = 10$ cards.

Since $10 > 9$, the landscape layout gives more cards.

**Answer: landscape**

cemc-fryer-2021-01c.title: Count the waste
cemc-fryer-2021-01c.body:
Portrait uses $15 \times 27$ cm of the page, i.e. $405$ cm² (9 cards). Landscape uses $18 \times 25$ cm, i.e. $450$ cm² (10 cards). Less waste means more cards: landscape.

**Answer: landscape**

cemc-fryer-2021-02a.title: Pythagorean Theorem
cemc-fryer-2021-02a.body:
The path is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 240 m (east) and 100 m (north): $\sqrt{240^2 + 100^2} = \sqrt{67\,600} = 260$ m.

**Answer: 260 m**

cemc-fryer-2021-02a.title: Scale a 5-12-13 triangle
cemc-fryer-2021-02a.body:
$100 : 240 = 5 : 12$, so the triangle is a $5$-$12$-$13$ triangle scaled by 20, and the hypotenuse is $13 \times 20 = 260$ m.

**Answer: 260 m**

cemc-fryer-2021-02b.title: Minute by minute
cemc-fryer-2021-02b.body:
In 3 minutes he walks 240 m; the last 20 m takes $\frac{20}{80} = \frac14$ minute. Total $3\frac14$ minutes.

**Answer: $3.25$ minutes**

cemc-fryer-2021-02c.title: Equal times
cemc-fryer-2021-02c.body:
$F$ and $G$ have the same $x$-coordinate, so $FG = 180 - 100 = 80$ m, and the halfway point is 40 m from each home.

- Franklin walks $260 + 40 = 300$ m at 80 m/min, taking $\frac{300}{80} = \frac{15}{4}$ minutes.
- Giizhig's path to her home is $\sqrt{240^2 + 180^2} = 300$ m, and then 40 m more: 340 m in total.

They take the same time, so $g = 340 \div \frac{15}{4} = \frac{1360}{15} = \frac{272}{3} \approx 90.67$.

**Answer: $g = \frac{272}{3}$**

cemc-fryer-2021-02c.title: Ratio of speeds
cemc-fryer-2021-02c.body:
In the same time, distances are proportional to speeds: $\frac{g}{80} = \frac{340}{300}$, so $g = 80 \cdot \frac{17}{15} = \frac{272}{3}$.

**Answer: $g = \frac{272}{3}$**

cemc-fryer-2021-03a.title: Reverse the first three
cemc-fryer-2021-03a.body:
The first three numbers $5, 2, 3$ become $3, 2, 5$; the rest stay: $3, 2, 5, 1, 4, 6$.

**Answer: $3, 2, 5, 1, 4, 6$**

cemc-fryer-2021-03b.title: Look at what changed
cemc-fryer-2021-03b.body:
Only the first four numbers moved. $R_4$ gives $4, 3, 2, 1, 5, 6$, and then $R_2$ swaps the first two: $3, 4, 2, 1, 5, 6$. ✓

**Answer: $R_4$ followed by $R_2$**

cemc-fryer-2021-03b.title: Work backwards
cemc-fryer-2021-03b.body:
The last operation must undo something to reach $3, 4, 2, 1, 5, 6$. Undoing $R_2$ (it is its own inverse) gives $4, 3, 2, 1, 5, 6$, which is $R_4$ applied to $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6$. (Other choices, like undoing $R_3$ or $R_4$, give $2, 4, 3, 1, 5, 6$ or $1, 2, 4, 3, 5, 6$, which are not a single reversal of the original.)

**Answer: $R_4$ followed by $R_2$**

cemc-fryer-2021-03c.title: Only R6 changes the last position
cemc-fryer-2021-03c.body:
**(i)** $R_3$: $3, 2, 1, 4, 5, 6$; then $R_6$: $6, 5, 4, 1, 2, 3$. So 2 operations suffice.

**(ii)** Every $R_n$ with $n < 6$ leaves the last number unchanged; $R_6$ moves the *first* number to the last position. So 3 can reach the last position only via an $R_6$ performed when 3 is first. In the original list 3 is not first, so a single operation cannot work.

Hence $m = 2$. ∎

cemc-fryer-2021-03d.title: Three work, two don't
cemc-fryer-2021-03d.body:
**Three suffice:** $R_5$: $5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 6$; $R_2$: $4, 5, 3, 2, 1, 6$; $R_6$: $6, 1, 2, 3, 5, 4$. ✓

**Two are not enough:** as in (c), 4 can only reach the last position by an $R_6$ applied when 4 is first. So with two operations, the first must bring 4 to the front — only $R_4$ does that — and the second must be $R_6$. But $R_4, R_6$ gives $4, 3, 2, 1, 5, 6 \to 6, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4$, whose second-last number is 3, not 5. One operation clearly can't work either (the original 4 is not first).

So the minimum is 3.

**Answer: 3**

cemc-fryer-2021-03d.title: Another 3-step sequence
cemc-fryer-2021-03d.body:
$R_6, R_3, R_6$: $6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 \to 4, 5, 6, 3, 2, 1 \to 1, 2, 3, 6, 5, 4$. ✓ The argument that 2 operations are impossible is the same as in Solution 1.

**Answer: 3**

cemc-fryer-2021-04a.title: Build it from the constraints
cemc-fryer-2021-04a.body:
Label the bottom vertices $b_0 = S, b_1, \ldots, b_6 = Y$ and the top vertices $t_0, t_1, \ldots, t_6 = F$, so $X = t_2$.

- $t_0$ has only the neighbours $S$ and $t_1$, so the path must go $S \to t_0 \to t_1$.
- From $t_1$ we can't go to $X = t_2$, so go down to $b_1$, then right to $b_2$.
- $b_2$'s other neighbours are $X$ (forbidden) and $b_3$: go to $b_3$, then up to $t_3$ (we need to visit $t_3$, and its only other neighbours are $X$ and $t_4$).
- $t_3 \to t_4 \to b_4 \to b_5 \to t_5 \to t_6 = F$, skipping $Y = b_6$.

So the path is $S, t_0, t_1, b_1, b_2, b_3, t_3, t_4, b_4, b_5, t_5, F$: up, right, down, right, right, up, right, down, right, up, right.

cemc-fryer-2021-04b.title: Case analysis
cemc-fryer-2021-04b.body:
Label the remaining vertices: $W$ between $S$ and $B$ on the bottom row; $X$ (right of $C$), $Y$ (right of $X$) and $G$ (below $F$) on the middle row; $Z$ between $A$ and $F$ on the top row. The edges are $S$–$W$–$B$, $C$–$X$–$Y$–$G$, $A$–$Z$–$F$ (rows) and $S$–$C$, $W$–$X$–$A$, $B$–$Y$–$Z$, $G$–$F$ (columns).

**The path must start $S \to C$.** $C$'s only neighbours are $S$ and $X$. If the path started $S \to W$, it could only enter $C$ from $X$ and then would be stuck (its other neighbour $S$ is used). So the path starts $S \to C \to X$.

From $X$ there are three options:

- **$X \to A$:** $A$'s other neighbour is $Z$; to also visit $B$ the path must go $A \to Z \to Y \to B \to W$, and now $W$'s neighbours $S, X, B$ are all used — stuck.
- **$X \to Y$:** to reach both $A$ and $B$, it goes either $Y \to Z \to A$ (then $A$'s neighbours $X, Z$ are used — stuck) or $Y \to B \to W$ (then $W$'s neighbours are used — stuck).
- **$X \to W$:** then $W \to B \to Y \to Z \to A$, and $A$ is a dead end.

In every case the path cannot visit $A$, $B$, $C$ and still reach $F$. ∎

cemc-fryer-2021-04c.title: Split at the middle column
cemc-fryer-2021-04c.body:
Call the column where the two rows overlap the *middle column*, with vertices $P$ (top left), $T$ (top right), $Q$, $U$ (middle left/right), $R$, $V$ (bottom left/right). Every $SF$ path enters the middle column from the left at $Q$ or $R$ and leaves to the right from $T$ or $U$.

**Inside the middle column**, list the possibilities:
- $Q \to T$: $QPT$, $QUT$, $QRVUT$ — 3 ways.
- $Q \to U$: $QU$, $QPTU$, $QRVU$ — 3 ways.
- $R \to T$: $RQPT$, $RQUT$, $RVUT$, $RVUQPT$ — 4 ways.
- $R \to U$: $RQU$, $RQPTU$, $RVU$ — 3 ways.

**Outside the middle column.** Let $M$ and $N$ be the vertices one unit to the left of $Q$ and $R$. In the 18 squares from $S$ up to $MN$, a path can't go backwards (it would revisit a vertex), so it is determined by choosing, in each square, its top or bottom edge; the vertical edges are then forced. That gives $2^{18}$ ways to arrive at $M$ or $N$ from the left. Each of them extends in exactly one way to $Q$ ($M \to Q$, or $N \to M \to Q$) and in exactly one way to $R$. So there are $2^{18}$ ways to reach $Q$ from the left, and $2^{18}$ ways to reach $R$. Symmetrically, there are $2^{18}$ ways to continue from $T$ (or from $U$) to $F$.

Total: $2^{18} \cdot (3 + 3 + 4 + 3) \cdot 2^{18} = 13 \cdot 2^{36}$.

**Answer: $13 \cdot 2^{36}$**

cemc-fryer-2021-04c.title: Small cases and a pattern
cemc-fryer-2021-04c.body:
Let $N(n)$ be the count when each row has $n$ squares. A computer search (or careful hand count) gives $N(2) = 13$, $N(3) = 52$, $N(4) = 208$: each extra square in each row doubles the count, because outside the middle column every square offers an independent top/bottom choice. So $N(n) = 13 \cdot 2^{2(n-2)}$ and $N(20) = 13 \cdot 2^{36}$.

**Answer: $13 \cdot 2^{36}$**
